options.text: Every object has its own box
If more objects than boxes exist, one box must contain more than one object

explanation: Put 13 people in a room and two of them share a birth month, because there are only 12 months. That is the whole principle: more objects than boxes forces at least one box to hold two. Formally, n objects into m boxes with n greater than m means some box holds at least the ceiling of n over m. It is one of the few results in this course you can be certain of without calculating anything.

why.a: Wrong, and it is the opposite: the principle applies precisely when there are not enough boxes to go round.
why.b: Correct. More objects than boxes forces at least one box to hold more than one.
why.c: Wrong. The principle says nothing about boxes being empty.
why.d: Wrong. Grouping is exactly what it is about.

options.text: Elements in A but not in B
Elements in B but not in A

explanation: Read the minus sign as take away: start with A, remove anything that is also in B. So A minus B keeps what is left of A. It is NOT symmetric, and that is the trap: A minus B and B minus A are different sets, which is why one of the wrong options is simply the reverse.

why.a: Wrong. Intersection keeps what is in BOTH; difference throws that part away.
why.b: Correct. Start with A, remove anything also in B.
why.c: Wrong, and it is B minus A, the reverse. Difference is not symmetric.
why.d: Wrong. Union keeps everything from both sets.

prompt: Truth set of a predicate is:

options.text: All values that make it false
All values that make the predicate true

explanation: A predicate such as P(x): x is greater than 3 is neither true nor false until x is given a value. Its TRUTH SET is the collection of values from the domain that make it true, here 4, 5, 6 and so on. The name says it: the set of things that make it TRUE. It is also the bridge between this module and sets, since it turns a logical statement into a set.

why.a: Wrong, and exactly inverted: those values form the complement of the truth set.
why.b: Correct. The values in the domain that make the predicate true.
why.c: Wrong. Nothing about it is random; it is fully determined by the predicate and the domain.
why.d: Wrong. The truth set is empty only when nothing satisfies the predicate, which is a special case rather than the definition.

prompt: The intersection A and B contains:

options.text: All elements of A and B
Only common elements of A and B

explanation: Intersection is the overlap: only what belongs to BOTH. The symbol is worth using as the hook, because the intersection symbol points up like the letter A in And, while the union symbol is a cup that holds everything. And means both, or means either.

why.a: Wrong. Everything from both sets is the UNION.
why.b: Correct. Only the elements common to both.
why.c: Wrong. That is closer to A minus B.
why.d: Wrong. That is closer to B minus A.

prompt: An infinite set is one that:

options.text: Has a countable number of elements

explanation: An infinite set is one whose elements never run out: the natural numbers, the integers, the even numbers. Work by elimination here, because three of the four options describe sets that clearly DO run out: no elements, five elements, ten elements. Only one option is left. Be aware that the wording is loose: countable is the word the manual uses for a set you can list off one by one, such as the naturals, which is countably infinite. It is not the sharpest definition, but it is the only option here that is not plainly finite.

why.a: Wrong. A set with no elements is the EMPTY set, and it is finite.
why.b: Wrong. That is a five-element set, as finite as they come.
why.c: Correct by elimination, and it matches the manual's wording for a set that can be listed off endlessly.
why.d: Wrong. Exactly ten elements is finite by definition.

prompt: A proper subset A of B means:

options.text: A is subset of B but not equal to B

explanation: PROPER means strictly smaller: every element of A is in B, and B has at least one element A does not. Compare the two symbols and the pattern is the same as with numbers: the plain subset symbol is like less than or equal to, and the proper subset symbol is like strictly less than. So every proper subset is a subset, and a set is a subset of itself but never a proper subset of itself.

why.a: Correct. Contained in B, and strictly smaller than B.
why.b: Wrong. Equal is the one case PROPER rules out.
why.c: Wrong. B being empty is unrelated, and would force A to be empty too.
why.d: Wrong, and impossible: a subset can never have more elements than the set containing it.

options.text: Elements in the universal set not in A

explanation: Everything outside A, measured against the UNIVERSAL set. That last part is essential: complement is meaningless without knowing what universe you are working in. The complement of the even numbers is the odd numbers if the universe is the integers, but something quite different if the universe is all real numbers. Always ask what the universal set is before answering.

why.a: Wrong. That is closer to the universal set itself.
why.b: Correct. Everything in the universal set that is not in A.
why.c: Wrong, and exactly backwards: that is A.
why.d: Wrong. The complement is empty only when A IS the universal set.

prompt: The symbol for the existential quantifier means:
explanation: There exists, the EXISTENTIAL quantifier, and one example is enough to make it true. Its partner is the universal quantifier, for all, which needs every case and is destroyed by a single counterexample. The shapes are the memory hook: the existential symbol is a backwards E for Exists, the universal one is an upside-down A for All.

why.a: Wrong. Therefore is a different symbol entirely, three dots in a triangle.
why.b: Correct. There exists, the existential quantifier.
why.c: Wrong. Not equal is an equals sign with a stroke through it.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the OTHER quantifier: for all is the upside-down A.

prompt: A predicate becomes a proposition when:

options.text: Variables are replaced with specific values

explanation: A proposition must be definitely true or definitely false. P(x): x is greater than 3 is neither, until you say x = 5, at which point it is true. So substituting a value turns a predicate into a proposition. Quantifying it does the same job the other way: for all x, P(x) is also a proposition, because it makes a definite claim about the whole domain.

why.a: Wrong, and it confuses cause with effect: a predicate with no variables was never a predicate.
why.b: Wrong. Connectives join statements; they do not settle a truth value.
why.c: Correct. Give the variables specific values and it becomes true or false.
why.d: Wrong. Always false is still a truth value, but that is not what makes it a proposition.

prompt: A subset A of B means:

options.text: A has more elements than B
All elements of A are in B
All elements of B are in A

explanation: Every element of A is also in B. Read the symbol from left to right and it points the right way round: the smaller set is on the left, the bigger on the right. Watch the direction, because one wrong option is the same claim reversed, and reversing it is the single most common slip in the topic.

why.a: Wrong. Disjoint means they share NOTHING, which is nearly the opposite.
why.b: Wrong, and impossible for a subset.
why.c: Correct. Every element of A is in B.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the reverse: that would make B the subset of A.

prompt: Biconditional p if and only if q is TRUE when:

options.text: p and q have same truth value

explanation: The biconditional is TRUE when both sides agree: both true, or both false. Read it as p equals q for truth values. It is the only connective in the course that is an equality test, which is why it is the one used to state logical equivalences.

why.a: Wrong. q true and p false makes the two sides disagree, so it is false.
why.b: Wrong. p being false is fine, provided q is false too.
why.c: Correct. True when both agree, false when they differ.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the mirror of the first wrong option: p true with q false is a disagreement.

prompt: An implication p implies q is FALSE when:

options.text: p is true and q is false
Both p and q are true
Both p and q are false
p is false and q is true

explanation: An implication is false in exactly ONE row of its truth table: true antecedent, false consequent. Everything else is true, including the two rows where p is false, which people find deeply unnatural. The hook is a promise: if it rains, I will bring an umbrella. You have only broken the promise if it rained and you turned up without one. If it did not rain, you cannot have broken it, whatever you carried.

why.a: Correct. True premise and false conclusion is the one broken case.
why.b: Wrong. True and true is a kept promise.
why.c: Wrong. It did not rain and you brought no umbrella, so nothing was broken. This is vacuously true.
why.d: Wrong. It did not rain and you brought one anyway, which breaks nothing.

explanation: Single is in the name. One thing worth keeping straight for a later question: the set containing the empty set is a SINGLETON, because it has exactly one element, and that element happens to be the empty set. So its cardinality is 1, not 0.

why.b: Wrong. That is an infinite set.
why.c: Wrong. No elements is the EMPTY or null set.
why.d: Wrong. Two elements would be a pair.

prompt: The conjunction p and q is TRUE when:

options.text: Either p or q is true
Both p and q are true
Both p and q are false

explanation: Conjunction is AND, and AND is the strict one: every part must hold. It is true in exactly one row out of four. Its partner disjunction, OR, is the generous one: true in three rows out of four, false only when both parts fail. Learn them as a pair, one strict and one generous.

why.a: Wrong. Either one being true is the definition of OR, not AND.
why.b: Wrong. If p is false the conjunction is false, whatever q does.
why.d: Wrong. Both false is the one row where even OR fails.

prompt: The union A or B contains:

options.text: All elements in A or B or both

explanation: Everything from either set, counted once. The phrase OR BOTH matters: this is the inclusive or of logic, not the everyday exclusive one, so an element in both sets still belongs and is listed a single time. That single counting is exactly why the inclusion-exclusion principle has to subtract the intersection.

why.a: Correct. Everything in A, everything in B, each counted once.
why.d: Wrong. Only the common elements is the INTERSECTION.
